One-line judgment: a choreographer does not just put a few moves to music, but turns an aesthetic idea into a movement plan that can be taught, rehearsed and reproduced, and carries it through with dancers and producers in rehearsal and performance; O*NET defines the occupation as creating new dance works, rehearsing the production and possibly directing and staging it.

Signals to keep exploring: you can keep revising your own plan under time and stamina constraints, and you are willing to break movement down into instructions someone else can learn; the O*NET work context shows that 100% answer that the work brings them physically very close to others, 76% have ongoing contact with others, 75% have face-to-face discussions every day, 57% stand continuously or almost continuously, 71% bend or twist continuously, and 57%
consider competition extremely intense. If you only want to perform and are unwilling to teach and revise, the gap will be large.

Conditions for pausing before a large investment: you have not yet led a full rehearsal of a complete segment in a real studio or class, and you have no movement notes or rehearsal records to show; choreographic work mostly comes as projects, short-term contracts or self-employment, with projects alternating with gaps and an unstable income structure, so you need to confirm first whether you can bear that rhythm.

United States: the BLS typical entry education is high school or equivalent, with dancer experience; some employers require or prefer a bachelor's degree. The O*NET certification discovery entry point showed no certification found in this round, which does not prove that all states, teaching activities or projects are licence-free; the specific position must be checked against local and employer requirements.
Mainland China: the Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Performances separately provide for licensing of performing groups and performance agency institutions, registration and filing for venues and individual performers or agents, and approval for holding performances; a choreographer who also holds, performs in or operates a performance must be checked according to the actual entity, and the organiser's procedures cannot be treated as a licence or exemption for all individuals in the occupation. Music, video and existing works are checked for copyright; identifiable images of people are additionally checked for portrait consent and statutory exceptions.

In one line: this is an occupation where whether the movement can be taught, whether it can be reproduced, whether the dancers' bodies are protected and whether time and venue can be scheduled decide success more than whether the inspiration is dazzling; if you are willing to revise a two-minute piece ten times and write clearly what each movement requires, it is worth serious consideration.

The work of a choreographer can be divided into three connected but distinct work dimensions. The first is creation and material: reading the script and music, studying characters and styles, drawing on other art forms, trying out different dancers and movements and positions, and recording influences and sketches. The second is rehearsal and direction: breaking movement down into teachable content, leading rehearsals, correcting technique, explaining breathing and rhythm and safety points, and adjusting according to dancer feedback and stamina. The third is presentation and collaboration: choosing music and sound or narrative, collaborating with
production roles such as music and costume and lighting, directing and staging the performance, and assessing the ability of students or dancers and taking part in selection.
Form a rehearsable movement plan and work structure

Clarify the creative goals and the presentation setting, study the music and text and character emotions, try out movement material and positions and record a reusable version, fix the structure and duration and transitions, write movement and rehearsal notes that dancers and producers can understand, and confirm the constraints of venue and music and costume and safety with the producers
Organize rehearsals and guide dancers to present safely

Break the rehearsal goals down by segment and set the schedule, lead warm-ups and progressive intensity and explain the stopping conditions, demonstrate and correct technique and handle individual differences, observe the presentation and record the passages that need revision, confirm with the dancers the feasible limits of music and positions and props and costume, and review the rehearsal and fix the next round of changes

Direct or take part in staging and maintain the work's versions; check the scope of copyright and portrait and contractual authorization for music and video and existing works; keep rehearsal notes and version records so that the work can be reproduced when you are not present.

Common adjacent positions include dancers, art and design directors, directors and producers, postsecondary art and drama and music teachers, self-enrichment teachers and dance teachers. On the boundaries: dancers output execution and interpretation of choreography; art directors and directors coordinate the whole work or the visual direction; teachers focus on teaching and training; choreographers output the movement plan and the rehearsal result and carry creative and directorial responsibility.
Turn an aesthetic idea into a movement plan and work structure that can be taught, rehearsed and reproduced
Dancers output bodily execution and interpretation of choreography; this occupation is responsible for the movement language and rehearsal notes and the stage presentation

Based on music and text and character emotion and spatial conditions, and preserving the creative process through records and sketches and versions; the O*NET work activities are led by thinking creatively, guiding and motivating subordinates, and performing general physical activities
Directors or producers coordinate the whole work and the production resources; this occupation is responsible for the movement language and rehearsal of the dance sections
Reading and research, generating movement material, arranging space and positions, organizing rehearsals, observing and revising, and directing and staging
Art and design directors are responsible for the overall visual and style direction; this occupation realizes and maintains consistency within the dance sections
Movement and rehearsal notes, version records and sketches, dancer feedback records, performance segments and presentation plans, casting and assessment records
Teachers output courses and training plans for learners; this occupation outputs works and rehearsal results for performance

Choreographers make creative and rehearsal decisions according to project duties; dancers execute within their ability and safety limits, and injuries are assessed by qualified medical personnel. For commercial performances in China, the host unit and the venue operator each have approval, verification and safety duties; a choreographer who also hosts, performs in or operates a performance must check the actual obligations, which cannot all be attributed to the organiser.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether the movement can be taught and reproduced; whether dancers' safety and stamina are protected; whether versions and revisions are recorded; whether music and video and existing works have been authorized; whether time and venue and production conditions can be scheduled; and whether the delivery is within the contract and duties.
Judgment one: whether the movement can be taught and reproduced

Break movement down into instructions others can learn (beats and breathing and centre of gravity and eye line and positions), and keep version records; missing understandable movement notes increase the difficulty for others to learn, for replacing dancers and for restaging; this cannot be used to assert that a work can definitely not be reproduced.
Judgment two: whether dancers' safety and stamina are protected

Editorial advice: design warm-ups, progression and rest according to the specific dance style, the dancers' ability and the venue arrangements, and check the floor, props and costume; IADMS states that the warm-up must suit the dance activity that follows. Pain or injury signals cannot be judged as grounds to continue by AI or by the checklist on this page; pause the relevant movements and have them assessed by qualified personnel, and in an emergency follow the local emergency pathway without waiting for the project's routine arrangements.
Judgment three: whether versions and revisions are recorded

For each revision, write down the change, the reason and the scope of impact; missing version records increase the difficulty of rehearsal, production handover and restaging checks, and the absence of records is not equated with an inability to restore the work.
Judgment four: whether music and video and existing works have been authorized

Before using music, video, existing works or recording dancers in rehearsal, confirm the copyright and contract and portrait and authorization scope; being visible online does not equal having permission, and the authorization scope for public performance and recording may differ.
Judgment five: whether time and venue and production conditions can be scheduled

Align rehearsal hours with venue availability and the load-in and dress rehearsal windows, and write the delivery times for music and costume and lighting into the plan; when conditions are incomplete, scale down rather than compressing safety and preparation time.
Judgment six: whether the delivery is within the contract and duties

Clarify the deliverables agreed in the contract (work plan, rehearsal direction, staging direction or restaging licence) and the credit and secondary use terms; work outside the scope should be priced and authorized before it is carried out.

Choreographers create new dance works and rehearse the production, and may direct and stage the presentation; the typical cycle is reading the script or setting the creative goal, studying the music and characters, generating movement material, arranging the stage space, organizing rehearsals, observing the performance and revising according to dancer feedback and production conditions.

O*NET-SOC 27-2032.00 (Choreographers; Bright Outlook, 2026 update) defines the occupation as creating new dance works, rehearsing the production and possibly directing and staging the presentation; the interest codes are AS (Artistic, Social), the preparation level is Job Zone Three, and the SVP range is 6.0 to below 7.0.

entries: Creation and material｜Generate movement material and record the creative process｜Try out different dancers and movements and positions, draw influences from other art forms such as drama and visual art and architecture, and record ideas and sketches and references to form reusable material (corresponding to O*NET tasks: trying out different dancers and movements and positions, drawing influences from other art forms, and developing creative ideas and keeping notes and sketches).

Rehearsal and direction｜Lead rehearsals and guide dancers' technique and safety｜Direct rehearsals to guide dancers in completing movements and achieving the intended effect, advise on standing and moving and teach correct technique to help prevent injury, and teach rhythm and interpretive movement to students and dancers and other performers (corresponding to tasks: directing rehearsals, instructing on standing and moving, and teaching rhythm and interpretive movement).

Work design｜Design dance for different settings and populations｜Design dance for individual dancers and companies and musicals and opera and fashion shows and film and television and special events, for populations ranging from beginners to professional dancers; choose music and sound or narrative to accompany the dance (corresponding to tasks: designing dance for different settings and populations, and choosing music and sound or narrative).

Presentation and direction｜Direct and stage the presentation｜Direct and stage dance presentations for different entertainment forms; collaborate with performers and production staff to design sets and lighting and costume and other artistic elements; coordinate with the music director to produce the music (corresponding to tasks: directing and staging the presentation, collaborating on artistic elements, and coordinating with the music director).

Casting and assessment｜Take part in selection and assess ability and areas for improvement｜Select performers for dance roles and assess students' dance ability to identify what needs improvement or adjustment (corresponding to tasks: selecting performers for roles, and assessing student ability).

Restaging and self-maintenance｜Restage traditional works and maintain your own technique｜Restage traditional dances and works in a company's repertoire and develop new interpretations; maintain technical proficiency and stamina and physical health through training and practice and classes; and manage or help manage a dance school (corresponding to tasks: restaging traditional works, maintaining technical proficiency and stamina, and managing a dance school).

paragraphs: The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: understanding of body and rhythm, collaboration with people, and organizational experience of rehearsal and presentation. The real differences lie in the output (a work plan, or a performance or course), the authority (creative decisions, or production coordination or teaching decisions) and the form of employment (projects and short-term contracts, or an institutional position). When choosing, it is better to test with one deliverable rehearsal segment and version record than to compare titles.

The basis for comparison is the task and work activity descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 27-2032.00 page, the adjacent occupation notes registered in this evidence route, and the public occupational materials for each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial compilation and does not constitute a conclusion about scope of practice or exchange of qualifications.

The table below compares positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: dancers, directors and producers, art and design directors, postsecondary art and drama and music teachers, self-enrichment teachers and teaching coordinators. The four columns each answer the same kind of question: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

Dancers output bodily execution and interpretation of choreography and carry performance responsibility; this occupation outputs the movement plan and rehearsal notes and the stage presentation, and the two differ in evaluation criteria and creative authority.
People willing to refine bodily expression over the long term are suited to the dancer direction; people willing to design movement and organize rehearsals are suited to this occupation.
Execute and interpret choreography with the body, with outputs mainly stage performance and rehearsal performance.
Dancers

Directors or producers coordinate the whole work and the production resources and carry production responsibility; this occupation is responsible for the movement language and rehearsal of the dance sections, at a different level and with different authority in the production chain.
People willing to coordinate the whole work and the production resources are suited to the director or producer direction; people willing to focus on dance creation are suited to this occupation.
Coordinate the overall direction of the work and the production resources, with outputs mainly the complete work and the production plan.
Directors and producers

Art and design directors are responsible for the overall visual and style direction and are usually engaged by an institution or client; this occupation realizes and maintains consistency within the dance sections.
People willing to decide the overall visual and style direction are suited to the art director direction; people willing to create within dance are suited to this occupation.
Determine the overall visual and style direction, with outputs mainly visual plans and style standards.
Art and design directors
Postsecondary art and drama and music teachers focus on courses and teaching and assessment and usually require the corresponding education; this occupation outputs works and rehearsal results.
People willing to do teaching and curriculum design over the long term are suited to the teacher direction; people willing to deliver works as the main output are suited to this occupation.
Take on curriculum design and teaching and assessment, with outputs mainly courses and teaching results.
Postsecondary art and drama and music teachers
Self-enrichment teachers work with non-professional learners on interests and basic skills; this occupation works towards a performance or a commission and is answerable for the result of the work.
People who like bringing dance to ordinary learners are suited to the self-enrichment course direction; people willing to carry the pressure of a work are suited to this occupation.
Teach interested learners, with outputs mainly courses and learner progress.
Self-enrichment teachers

Teaching coordinators are responsible for the curriculum system and teaching management and scheduling and usually do not carry creative duties; this occupation's responsibility lies with the work and the rehearsals.
People willing to work on the curriculum system and teaching management are suited to the teaching coordination direction; people willing to create and lead rehearsals are suited to this occupation.
Coordinate courses and teaching resources and scheduling, with outputs mainly teaching plans and management reports.
Teaching coordinators

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires filling in new abilities and evidence: the dancer direction requires continuous performance and physical condition, the director and producer direction requires production and budget and coordination experience, the art director direction requires overall visual and style judgment, and the teaching direction requires curriculum design and assessment ability. Movement language and rehearsal organization transfer, but each direction requires accumulating presentable results again.

paragraphs: Boundary: the six risk cards below are summarized from this occupation's tasks and work context, to explain what you will encounter and how it can be controlled; they do not state incidence rates or accident probabilities, and the scope of application of each measure must be confirmed separately under the project contract and the venue and jurisdiction requirements.

The key pressures summarized editorially: rehearsal load and personnel safety, rights in music and video and existing works, income and expenditure arrangements across projects and gaps, and version handover, scheduling and venue conditions. They do not mean that injury, failed delivery or an unsustainable career is inevitable.

U.S. O*NET tasks and work context support the risk scenarios; the measures are editorial advice, not an incident rate. The BLS wage and employment sub-items for this occupation are checked separately; in China the operation, hosting and venue duties are checked under the Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Performances, and copyright and portrait rights are checked under the corresponding laws.
Choreographers who carry work creation and rehearsal direction

O*NET includes tasks of demonstrating technique, helping prevent injury and continuous physical activity; the IADMS warm-up material emphasizes preparation specific to the activity. The editorial risk check covers personnel ability, load, floor, props and costume; no incident rate for this occupation or individual causal effect of these factors was obtained, and the checklist cannot guarantee safety.

Editorial advice is to arrange appropriate warm-up, progression and rest according to the dance style and individual ability, and to have unknown high-difficulty movements checked by the relevant professionals first rather than tried directly. When pain or injury signals appear, pause the relevant movements and have them assessed by qualified personnel; in an emergency follow the local emergency pathway immediately without waiting for routine project referral. This page does not set recovery standards.
Skipping warm-ups or compressing recovery time to catch up with the schedule; treating pushing through as professional.

If the copyright and portrait and contractual authorization for music, video, existing choreography and dancer rehearsal recordings are not confirmed, public performance or recorded release may face infringement and takedown risk.

Confirm the authorization scope and credit requirements early in creation, and distinguish the different authorizations for rehearsal use, public performance and recording; write the authorization status into the version record and retain written evidence.
Substituting visible online or used before for permission; using rehearsal material directly for promotional release.
Positions responsible for work versions and handover

Editorial risk scenario: insufficient movement notes and version records may increase the difficulty of restaging, touring, replacing dancers and checking handovers; it is not asserted that missing records necessarily make restoration impossible or cause delivery to fail.

For each revision, write the version number and the changes and the reason and the scope of impact clearly; write the movement notes to the level where someone else can rehearse from them, and keep the authoritative version where the project can access it.
Maintaining the work only through word of mouth and personal memory; leaving changes scattered in private chat records.
Choreographers who take on commissions and commercial projects

Editorial advice is to check delivery, the number of rehearsals, credit and the scope of secondary use to avoid disputes from additional requests; in China the ownership of commissioned works is determined under Article 19 of the Copyright Law and the contract, and not all rights can be attributed to the commissioning party.

Before taking on work, write clearly the deliverables and the number of rehearsals and dress rehearsals and travel and credit and secondary use and how out-of-scope work is billed; for requests outside the scope, settle the pay and authorization before carrying them out.
Editorial counter-example: relying only on unrecorded verbal communication to add revisions, reuse or change credit without confirming the scope; this does not mean all oral contracts are invalid.
Positions responsible for load-in and dress rehearsal windows

Editorial risk scenario: a compressed load-in and dress rehearsal window may hinder technical and personnel preparation; the specific safety standards and responsibility must be checked separately, and a reduced scale cannot be taken to mean it is safe. For commercial performances in China the venue and the host unit each perform the duties in Articles 17—23 of the regulations.

Editorial advice is to reserve time for checking the venue, lighting and sound and for the dress rehearsal; when conditions are insufficient, report first and check whether to adjust or postpone, and do not substitute a reduced scale for safety verification or decide unilaterally to suspend a commercial performance. Actual emergency handling follows the applicable regulations, plans and authorized positions.
Promising the presentation result before confirming the venue and technical conditions; trading compressed dress rehearsal time for more rehearsal.
Choreographers working on a project and self-employed basis

Editorial scenario: alternating projects and gaps may make self-employed income unstable; concentrated workloads may also increase fatigue. BLS Table 1.2 shows 39.6% self-employment for U.S. choreographers in 2025 and provides no burnout rate or personal income projection.

Plan income and expenditure across projects and gaps on an annual basis and set aside reserves; develop parallel income sources related to teaching or production; arrange recovery periods and recognize the signs of exhaustion.

values: Fictional T1｜paper choreography only, without actually dancing or diagnosing old injuries; complete the first draft in 90 minutes.

Music M1: 4/4 time, 120 beats per minute, 16 beats in total, the first 8 beats calm and the last 8 turning firm; 16 beats = 8 seconds. The text is hesitating and stopping, then looking up to find a companion, then moving forward together; no additional audio is needed.

Stage plan: 8 m wide by 6 m deep, with the lower left corner at (0,0), the audience at y<0 and the side doors at (0,3)/(8,3). Paper positions
D1(2,2), D2(4,2), D3(6,2), D4(2,4), D5(4,4), D6(6,4); the side doors must not be blocked, and movement paths must avoid crossing at the same time.

D1—D6 are all fictional. The scenario stipulates that for D6, landing jumps, lifts and fast spins are prohibited; the conditions of a gymnasium without a dance floor have not been professionally confirmed, so all real movement rehearsal must be checked and a safe path drawn on paper does not mean the venue is safe.

4 rehearsals of 90 minutes each; the time template given is 10 minutes for condition checking, 15 warm-up, 25 low-intensity segments, 10 rest, 15 linking, 10 feedback and 5 minutes recording. Stop and hand over to the person in charge if there is pain, dizziness or an unconfirmed venue; this template is for paper scheduling only and is not a medical or training prescription.

Authorization U1: the commissioning party provides M1, permitting only one offline performance by this unit; internal review may see the rehearsal records of the named members but may not publish the video. Portrait consent, the music rights chain and further performances are not established in the question; they must be checked separately, and what the commissioning party provides cannot be treated as full authorization.
Task｜Deliver notes for 16 beats of movement and formations, a 4×90 minute plan, and a version and authorization list.

Write the centre of gravity, eye line, movement intention and formation for beats 1—4, 5—8, 9—12 and 13—16 group by group; provide a non-jumping alternative for D6; this alternative does not constitute clearance to perform movements with an injury. Mark the paths and the side doors, and check the total duration and the 90-minute allocation.

Assumed feedback F1: the paths of D2 and D5 cross when they exchange at beat 9; submit a v02 solution and the reason, keeping the v01 record. Under U1, list the material that may be seen internally, that is prohibited from publication and that requires separate checking.
Reference deliverable｜Several approaches are acceptable, provided the conditions and changes can be reviewed.

Duration 16÷120×60=8 seconds. Options: beats 1—4 change weight in place with gaze down, beats 5—8 look up towards the centre, beats 9—12 take a small step 0.5 m forward from the original position, and beats 13—16 face the audience steadily; D6 keeps the whole passage as a low-impact paper plan, and real feasibility is subject to professional checking.

Reference v02 cancels the D2/D5 exchange, keeping each person's x column, with all six moving 0.5 m in the negative y direction over beats 9—12; the corresponding end points are (2,1.5)/(4,1.5)/(6,1.5)/(2,3.5)/(4,3.5)/(6,3.5). The paper paths do not cross and the side doors (0,3)/(8,3) remain clear, but this does not prove real-world safety.

Each session is 90=10+15+25+10+15+10+5 minutes. Session 1 checks the conditions and beats 1—8, session 2 checks beats 9—16 and handles F1, session 3 links the passage within the conditions permitted and rechecks the D6 alternative, and session 4 rechecks the version and the authorization; do not compress warm-up or rest to make up progress.

Keep M1/U1/F1, v01/v02, the changed beat numbers, the reason, the responsible person and the date. Limited internal review is not public permission; public recording, portrait and further performances all require separate checking. Review covers the 16-beat coverage, the arithmetic, the handling of F1, the stopping conditions and the rights boundary, and is not scored on whether it can actually be danced.
Everything in the question is fictional; only paper plans, scheduling and rights checking.

No reader is required to actually dance, practise while injured, film others or upload unauthorized material; passing the simulation does not prove real choreography, safety, business or authorization qualifications.
Condition checklist｜M1/U1/D6 and the venue.

List each given condition, the evidence location and the items to be checked; mark the music rights chain, portrait consent, venue and professional assessment as unconfirmed, and do not invent permissions.
Review sheet｜16 beats and 8 seconds, 90 minutes per session.
Check 16÷120×60 and the sum of the 7 time blocks; check the six end points in v02, the non-crossing paths and the side doors, noting that paper does not equal actual safety.

entries.answer:
Daily tasks are mainly creation and rehearsal and collaboration: directing rehearsals to guide dancers in completing movements and achieving the intended effect, advising on standing and moving and teaching correct technique to help prevent injury, trying out different dancers and movements and positions and recording reusable material, designing dance for different settings and populations, choosing music and sound or narrative, directing and staging the presentation, and collaborating with production roles to design sets and lighting and costume. The O*NET work context shows that 100%
answer that the work brings them physically very close to others, 75% have face-to-face discussions every day, 57% stand continuously or almost continuously, and 71% bend or twist continuously.
entries.question: What do choreographers do every day?

entries.answer: Dancers output bodily execution and interpretation of choreography; directors and producers coordinate the whole work and the production resources; art and design directors are responsible for the overall visual and style direction; college teachers focus on courses and teaching; this occupation outputs the movement plan and rehearsal notes and the stage presentation, and carries creative and directorial responsibility. Shared capabilities do not mean the positions can be exchanged: creative authority, production responsibility and employment form all differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between choreographers and adjacent occupations?

entries.answer: That cannot be inferred. The core tasks of this occupation are turning a concept into movement others can learn, observing on site and adjusting immediately, judging dancer safety and stamina, and bearing responsibility for the work that must be delivered; these depend on long bodily experience and project responsibility. Generative tools can organize material and drafts, but cannot replace on-site judgment and the final choice.
entries.question: Will AI replace choreographers?

entries.answer: Editorial advice: material, structural drafts, versions and schedule documents can be tried with tool assistance; on-site direction, dancer condition and expression judgments need review. In this round no time series of task adoption was obtained, so no order of automation or substitution timeline is provided.
entries.question: Which choreographer tasks are most easily automated?

entries.answer: Breaking a concept into teachable, rehearsable movement, reading dancers' condition in the rehearsal studio and adjusting immediately, judging whether a movement exceeds a dancer's ability, and delivering the work and being responsible for the result. These abilities depend on bodily experience and collaborative trust, not on tool proficiency.
